assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices (BLP), and the dynamic-oligopoly framework built on it, became the standard toolkit for merger review, antitrust, and empirical industrial organization. The methodological contribution is clear, widely adopted, and has changed both academic and policy practice.
assessment.attribution: The 1995 demand-estimation paper is most closely tied to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also led the dynamic-games work (Ericson-Pakes and later papers). Bresnahan, Reiss and Benkard have strong claims, but a three-person cap leaves them out and makes the cut debatable.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The core methods date from the 1990s and have been applied and stress-tested for three decades. Practical problems such as numerical sensitivity and weak identification are well documented and have been largely addressed.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers to include Bresnahan, whose earlier empirical-IO work was influential, over Levinsohn.
Known numerical and identification sensitivities in BLP implementations, which affect how robust the applied results are.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the empirical work on import competition from China reshaped understanding of labour-market adjustment, wage polarization, and the distributional costs of trade. The work is highly influential in both academia and public debate.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock evidence is mainly Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The task framework draws on Autor with Levy and Murnane and on the Katz-Murphy skill-premium tradition. Lawrence Katz's credit is spread across these strands, and a three-name cap leaves it uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature (about 10 to 25 years of citation and debate). The core findings have been replicated and extended, though the magnitudes and long-run interpretation remain actively debated.
uncertainties: Debate over the size and persistence of local labour-market effects and over the identification strategy.
Overlap with the 2023 prize for work on gender and labour-market history, and with the Katz/Goldin lineage, complicates attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore credit cycles and the Bernanke-Gertler financial accelerator explain how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. This became the backbone of post-2008 macro-financial modelling and policy thinking.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clearest originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism. Gertler is central to the financial accelerator and later work, but Bernanke, who shared the 2022 prize, is not on this ballot. That makes the Gertler link an attribution question.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The foundational papers are from 1997 to 1999, and the framework has been widely applied, empirically tested and extended after the financial crisis.
uncertainties: Whether the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig reduces room for a closely related macro-finance award.
Direct empirical identification of the amplification mechanism is harder than the theory suggests.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Grossman-Helpman models of lobbying and protection formalized how special-interest politics shapes trade policy. They also link to their influential work on innovation and growth, so the combined body of work is large and central to trade theory and political economy.
assessment.attribution: The pairing is natural, because the key contributions are largely joint. The cleanest claim is the protection-for-sale model. Helpman's separate heterogeneous-firm work appears elsewhere on the list, which blurs how much credit belongs to each strand.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The central papers are from the 1990s, with decades of follow-on theory and empirical testing. Empirical support for the specific protection-for-sale predictions is mixed.
uncertainties: Mixed empirical tests of the protection-for-sale model.
Whether the Committee prefers to recognize Helpman through the firm-heterogeneity work rather than this strand.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A systematic theoretical and empirical programme on how constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy outcomes. It transformed political economics into a mainstream field with testable implications.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the main authors of the constitutional and electoral-rules programme. Besley has a strong claim through the state-capacity work and political agency. Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity could affect how the Committee reads the novelty of this award.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The programme has been developed since the 1990s, with a substantial body of empirical work, though much of the cross-country evidence relies on observational identification.
uncertainties: Causal identification in the cross-country constitutional evidence.
Partial overlap in subject matter with the 2024 prize, which may count against a second award in the area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities, interest-rate rules and optimal monetary policy is the dominant paradigm in central-bank policy analysis. Its practical and conceptual influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: Highly dispersed. Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets all have claims, and others not on the ballot (such as Rotemberg and Wouters) may too. Any three-person selection is contestable, and the choice here is a judgment call.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The framework has been used for over two decades, but its performance during the post-2008 and post-2020 inflation episodes has prompted renewed debate over its empirical adequacy.
uncertainties: Severe attribution dispersion among many plausible contributors.
Empirical performance concerns about the model's treatment of inflation and its reliance on strong auxiliary assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data was used to measure intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation, with causal neighbourhood-effect estimates, giving new descriptive and policy-relevant knowledge. The empirical design is transparent and the policy impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure across the programme. Hendren and Friedman are core co-authors on specific components, and Katz contributed to the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis. A three-name cap leaves reasonable room for disagreement.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The key results are about 10 years old and are still being replicated, extended to other countries, and debated. Some methodological critiques of the neighbourhood-effect estimates and mobility measures are still being worked through.
uncertainties: Robustness of place-based causal estimates and the interpretation of mobility measures.
Time since publication is shorter than for the older entries, so long-run replication and external validity evidence is still accumulating.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Models and experiments on reciprocity, fairness, and inequity aversion explained systematic departures from selfish behaviour in bargaining, public goods and contracts. They also reshaped contract theory and the design of institutions. The findings are among the more reproducible results in behavioural economics.
assessment.attribution: Fehr-Schmidt (1999) and the Fehr-Gächter punishment work are the clear anchors. Falk's contribution is substantial, but the two-name selection is cleaner. The award would overlap partly with earlier behavioural prizes (Kahneman and Smith in 2002, Thaler in 2017), though the subject area is distinct.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The foundational papers are from the late 1990s and early 2000s, with extensive replication and field extensions. Debates continue over the stability and external validity of social preferences. I work in an adjacent behavioural and experimental area, so I flag proximity to the subject without a personal connection to these candidates.
uncertainties: External validity of lab-measured social preferences and model-specific parametrizations.
Whether the Committee views the contribution as sufficiently distinct from earlier behavioural and experimental prizes.
